utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue your submissions under Rule 98 bis? By the way, the Chamber received in writing citations you've referred to at certain transcript pages. We do not consider to be a filing but just an aide-memoire to have this at hand easily for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful Your Honours received it. Thank you very much. Your Honour, I will now return to the submission under Rule 98 bis on behalf of Ivan Cermak. Yesterday I had reached the stage where I was dealing with the Article 7(3) allegation within the indictment, principally arising from paragraph 7 of the indictment, and I had dealt with the issue of the subordination of Croatian units as cited in the indictment with -- under Mr. Cermak. I'm now turning to the military police, and I will then, after that, deal with the civilian police, in relation to this same issue. The military police. Your Honour, it is clear from the hierarchy of the structure of the military police that General Cermak, as the garrison commander, was not included within the de jure organigram. If you look at D785 to 7, you will see there those exhibits where the structure of the military police is set out. It is quite clear that the military police orders that the military police structure, as it operated in Knin at that time, did not include General Cermak within its functioning. This Court has seen a large number of exhibits emanating from the military police administration, issued by General Lausic, emanating from the 72nd Battalion, under the control of either Major Juric or Colonel Budimir. None of those documents are referred to nor include General Cermak. You have also seen documents relating to the Knin company that was formed on the 5th of August established for the newly liberated territory. Again, not a single document within the workings and structure of that unit which is particularly cited in paragraph 7. No documents relating to General Cermak. We had called as a witness a man called Dzolic who was the commander of the Knin company of the military police at some time from the 5th of August to the 12th of August. Prosecution had called this witness specifically on the issue of whether the Knin company was at any time subordinated to General Cermak. What is interesting in the structure of their case against this accused, that if the Court looks at his statement, P875, the Court will see that in his original interviews none of the orders from General Cermak, as they have been described, to the military police were actually put to that witness, so that he, as a member of the Knin company, was never asked to lay a foundation for the central proposition. In the Prosecution pre-trial opening brief, as well as their opening address, the contents of their expert's report as to whether he was subordinated to General Cermak. None of those orders, and they are the famous UNCRO orders that the Court will have well in mind, P513, D788, P512, D303, D503, P509, none of them were put to that witness before he gave evidence here to establish, first of all, whether he had received them, and what his position on those documents were. Now, I don't know how these statements arise and how they're taken by the investigators, but it is clear that the Prosecution were in possession of the knowledge of those documents right from their first interview with General Forand. Why was there no explanation in the statement about that matter? Why was it that at paragraph 37, a rather woolly expression, the kind of expression that alerts a Defence counsel that there is something up. Why was there this expression? "The way I understood it was that I was still under the command of Colonel Budimir but that I was also under the command of General Cermak, and I was to obey any order that General Cermak gave me." Well, that sentence puts an Defence counsel immediately on a situation of alert, because the expression is odd, what it means is odd, and no one is grasping the nettle here in this statement and saying, What about this order? This order? This order? Those orders that perform the very basis of the Prosecution case against General Cermak. So if we look further into his statement when he gives an example of two trucks of the international Red Cross having been stolen, paragraph 44 of P875, what does he say? "Cermak and me at the meeting, and he told me that he had been informed by the international Red Cross," and so Mr. Dzolic went on to inform the military crime police. Paragraph 45: "I was called to Cermak's office like this on two or three occasions." He refers to the 9th August. "And he told me to go and visit. He told me to record any incidents of burning that I witnessed." Interesting about this is the way the word "order" is not used; it's telling. When the witness came and give evidence viva voce before this Court and was cross-examined by the Defence, he informed the Court that he was not subordinated, a key word in relation to this trial, to General Cermak, and in relation to those UNCRO orders that form the foundation of the case against him, and by that I mean against General Cermak, he said: "I, first of all, haven't seen any of the orders," that were put before him, transcript number 9020 up to 9025, and he said at 9028 he "was not obliged to follow orders of this kind as orders; however, as information that something had occurred." And that is the very point of this case, because, on the one hand, the Prosecution are saying in their indictment that General Cermak took no action in relation to reports of crimes to him. Here in paragraphs 44, 45, 46 of that witness's statement, he clearly demonstrates that at the meetings General Cermak had in the early stages in Knin when General Forand informed him about burning, about houses being set on fire, and that the military were involved, here you have it. General Cermak passing that information on, not because he was in command, but because he was passing it on as something that, as a responsible military officer, he should do. How does this set as a snapshot of evidence with the case against General Cermak? The witness himself never asked whether he was subordinated to him. The witness, never being shown these documents. And then when he is shown these documents, he gives a perfectly reasonable explanation that fits with the recording by him in his statement of being told to go and see what was happening. How does this also set with the allegation that General Cermak was in Knin denying crimes, taking no steps in relation to crime, minimizing crimes, and member of a joint criminal enterprise? Well, if he is doing these steps, how is he within the joint criminal enterprise? I refer to that here as the second part of my submission will be concerned with the Article the 7(1) allegations in the trial. But because we're here at the moment, I refer the Court to it, to forecast what is to come. The other foundation that the Prosecution have relied upon for command of the military police has been documents adduced prior to Operation Storm by their expert witness Mr. Theunens, all of which did not tell the full story as to the powers and responsibilities of a garrison commander. It was of interest to note that no documents after Operation Storm were produced to show the workings of the Split garrison, which was the particular garrison he was using as a comparison. Next, as I referred you to yesterday, he gave an example of a garrison commander disciplining a member of the Croatian military, and it was quite clear from the documents that we produced that the full story was that that was a subordinate of the garrison commander at Split, Colonel Zoricic. The other foundation that the Prosecution rely upon are the garrison regulations, as well as order and work and discipline in the garrison, which was an order passed in 1993 and put to General Lausic who was supposed to give evidence in support of the Prosecution theory. It turned out that General Lausic was unaware of the 1993 order concerning work, discipline, and organisation in the garrisons. Until he had been produced documents for him to review by the Prosecution investigator, Mr. Foster, the day before he gave evidence, he was unaware of that particular order. It was noticeable when he gave his evidence in-chief that Mr. Tieger took him very rapidly through the document and just asked him whether it was consistent or inconsistent with the rules of the military police of 1994, Article 8, and Article 9; Exhibit P880. He said consistent. What that means, I'm not entirely sure I understand. But when I cross-examined him and pointed out the non-operational nature of the garrison commander, it was clear he accepted that the garrison commander had only a very limited responsibility with the military police, and that was because the garrison was concerned with the internal functioning of an area where the military were based and the regulations and rules were designed to enable the army to function in an orderly way, as amongst itself and the local community, and that, in those terms, that gave the garrison commander his right to enforce his regulations. And the Court will recall my cross-examination of Mr. Theunens and the speeding over the weak bridge. Looking in more detail now at the relationship, as alleged, between General Cermak and the military police, one considers specifically the Knin company. General Lausic conceded that there had been no document that he had seen which showed that the Knin company had ever been subordinated to General Cermak, as would have been required by his order of the 14th of August, 1995, in which he told the commander of the 72nd to subordinate a company to the highest ranking Croatian military officer in the area. I don't have time here to go into the niceties of what the rules say concerning regular tasks, daily tasks, daily operational command, a phrase that General Lausic used, and the significance and variance of these expressions. But in our submission, they are important and we ask the Court to consider them, because we are discussing here the exercise of valid acts or not of subordination. Also, there is the issue, the issue concerning the position of the highest ranking officer by function in the area of responsibility. That key phrase was omitted from the first translation before this Court. After Dzolic gave evidence, the version of the 1994 military police rules was amended to include that important word that had been omitted. Lausic conceded that General Cermak would not have been the most senior commander by function in the region. Not only that, when you go to the documents that have been produced upon the Knin company, I've already referred to the fact that there is no sending on or copying or including of General Cermak or the Knin garrison into any such orders, but you look at the Knin company in operation after the 12th of August. Orders issued by Colonel Budimir appointing a Lieutenant Orsulic as the commander of the Knin company and also including the rotation of the units that constitute the Knin company, that was not referred to General Cermak. How can you command someone if you don't know who they are? These are basic principles. These were not internal documents. These were documents of appointment. They're also the only thing that the Court has to go on. None of them refer to General Cermak. The point was made on a number of occasions that he had to request others to have the military police provide a service to him. The Court will recollect the request for men in relation to his personal security. If General Cermak was in command of the Knin company, he could have just ordered that. All the evidence of the system in operation, as well as the testimony of the witnesses, have defied and contradicted this case that has been brought against him. I don't have time to go into it in a very precise and detailed way, but I refer the Court to our cross-examination of the witnesses Lausic, Theunens, Dzolic, and in a brief way, Simic, although he was not directly involved with the Knin company. The Court will recollect the daily reports. They were a curiosity because they were referred to the Split garrison commander, and the reason for that, as explained by General Lausic, was because the Split garrison had a duty service. And from there, they were able to inform the commander of the 72nd, Colonel Budimir, as to incidents that had happened. The Split garrison command was in the same command building as the 72nd command. Again, none of those documents referred to General Cermak. And this Court has been asked to accept that this man, in his position, was in command of all those units, including the military police, in this area. In our submission, it does not add up and make sense, and there is no forensic evidence to support the assertions. What we say is this: The Prosecution took a theory of this case from the international witnesses. Those international witnesses had limited knowledge. They produced some evidence and documents; hence, the orders relating to the recovery of the UNCRO vehicles. But, in fact, if this investigation, prior to trial, had concentrated on the reality rather than the hypothetical and looked in a more in-depth way into the workings of the Croatian military and civil system, it would have found the answers that we have provided during this trial as to how the system worked. What can be the reason for an investigator not putting the key military police orders that are -- that were the signature of Mr. Theunens' testimony. Many times when I asked him questions he would refer back to the UNCRO orders. And, Your Honour, Mr. President, said: "Yes, we know about the UNCRO orders. Is there anything else?" Every time that signature tune was played. But what is curious is, for the foundation of this case, that signature tune needed to be played to the people in possession of the actual knowledge, which were the Croatian witnesses. To have a court like this that receives evidence where one party chooses to ignore evidence emanating from a principal, the principal source for the basis of this trial, being the Croatian military system, its witnesses, how the system worked, before it developed a case theory, in our submission, is utterly astonishing. Let me now turn to the civilian police, which is the third arm of the Croatian system over which it is alleged Mr. Cermak had effective control. Well, again, through us, the Court were able to see organigrams of the police structure - Exhibits D231, Prosecution put one in, Exhibit P962, as to how the system worked. Witness 86 gave a clear list of important people in the Knin area over the months of August and September from the headquarters either in Zadar-Knin police administration, Split-Dalmatia police administration, or from the ministry in Zagreb, who were down there working with him. Smiljan Relic, transcript reference T5509; Franjo Djurica, 5531; Mr. Gledec, transcript 5512. I will just burn time if I list all those people in the hierarchy. Benko, Nad, Tomurad, Kardum, Batanga, Cetina, Moric, all who came down to Knin. Now, if Mr. Cermak was in effective control of the civilian police there would be something arising from those visits by those people connected to him. Not a single thing. And in fact the reason for this is quite obvious. The Croatian structure of government and its organs had a clear division between the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Interior, and they were separate hierarchies, and each relevant witness said they were from a separate hierarchy and the military could not control them. But let me just turn to that theme that I mentioned in relation to the military police. If this case has been built and constructed from the theories of the international witnesses who may have had great influence on the Prosecutor in preparing this indictment and its allegations, you are going to make that kind of mistake in your allegations against an accused, because the fact of the matter is not a single one of the international witnesses from General Forand down to the human rights team leaders, such as Mr. Flynn, all of them confessed to not knowing how the Croatian system operated. But if you take a case theory from that background, you are bound to start to make mistakes in the construction of a case and an indictment when you select an accused. Let us again look at the background documents, many emanating from the Kotar-Knin police administration, Zadar-Knin police administration, from Mr. Moric as the assistant minister for the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb, none of them copied in to General Cermak. None of them in any way reflecting that he had an effective control over the police. How can you have a system operating if someone who has an effective control such that the institution is subordinated to him, if he doesn't know what is going on, if is he not a part of the operation of that machinery. We introduced into this case hundreds of documents showing the system at work, from the clearance of the terrain, the setting up of check-points, inspections, controls, joint activities between UNCIVPOL and the local police. Nowhere was Mr. Cermak to be found. So how is it that this allegation would arise? Well, the pre-trial brief has that signature tune of the UNCRO orders issued by General Cermak, in relation to the loss of vehicles, et cetera. So what was said about that by the key witnesses? Because those key witnesses have to support this theory by the Prosecution, if they are to have any chance of establishing criminal liability, and we say that this issue demonstrates why, again, this case fails. Interestingly enough, Witness 86 was asked about this matter, and one refers to his statement. And, again, those UNCRO orders were not put before that witness in his statement. Not there. Why not there? In fact, that witness, in his statement said, "General Cermak never gave me direct orders; however, sometimes conclusions were reached." Paragraph 65 of Exhibit P487. "I did feel, however, that's was answerable to him." Well, how on earth does this go any -- any part or step towards establishing a subordination of effective control? What is going on here in the creation of this case against this accused? Why was it gone so wrong? Why is the case theory absolutely in contradiction to the evidence that is there? Did the evidence get any better in cross-examination? Answer, it got better for the Defence but worse for the Prosecution. Because, unlike the Prosecution, we put every single order to the witness, and he said, "this was information." "This was information," he said. "I didn't have to take orders." Well, it beggers belief that we're standing here spending all this money on this trial, and we have such fundamental problems in the case theory, its presentation, and the evidence. If I am addressing at the close of the Prosecution case the Judges about such fundamental issues as this. They were -- I didn't have to act on them. Well, there we are. He chose to express for the first time here fully how he viewed the situation, and the Court has now received the evidence. That is the purpose, as I understand it, of these proceedings, is to extract from a trial that shouldn't be happening against an accused, an accused wrongly -- wrongly charged and put on an indictment in relation to crimes such as these. Looking at that statement again, Defence counsel reading it immediately would be alerted under Exhibit P487 and Exhibit P489 about how the content, in relation to the Prosecution case theory, and what this witness had to say was never explicitly dealt with. It's all around the edges. It is giving an impression, the kind of impression the Court heard in opening from my learned friend Mr. Tieger. When you dig and look at it, it does not add up. Not only that, there was corroboration for this evidence. Court will remember two documents that were produced by the Defence from the Knin police station referring to the UNCRO orders that had been issued by General Cermak. How, then, was that described? Commander Mijic, in the first document, which was a very poor reproduction, refers to the order. The second document clearly states a complaint has been filed by the commander of the Knin garrison concerning the UNCRO vehicles. A complaint. Well, you're damned if you do, and you're damned if you don't, in this case, it seems to me. You pass on and report crimes are happening, and then it is said that you have a command authority, effective command. You don't do it, and you're accused of not reporting, covering up, minimizing, denying crimes. The Court, in our submission, has to look very carefully at this. This cannot be an impossible situation, a Kafka nightmare, where if you report it's said that you have a control. If you pass on information, you have control; if you don't, you're apparently covering up. And we refer the Court very carefully to those passages that indicate that there was no effective control and superior/subordinate relationship between General Cermak and the local police in Knin. Your Honours, that's a halfway point for me now, as between Article 7(3) and Article 7(1) in my submissions, and I will now turn to deal with Article 7(1), which is the joint criminal enterprise allegation. A few general matters. A plurality of persons, more than one, to include the accused is required to establish a joint criminal enterprise. That has as a basis for its proposition the fact whether there was or not a joint criminal enterprise. This is a case which has a clear background of a revenge motive by the civilian population, individual military personnel and others against those Serbs who had remained in the Serbian Krajina, as they called it, and who had, themselves, expelled large numbers of Croatians from this area in 1991, 1992, and afterwards, and caused them to live in a reduced version of their country, had kept them in a bottleneck, unable to get to their homes, and, indeed, to impose great hardship upon them. This background is very clear in this case. And in our submission, this Court has to be satisfied that those named from President Tudjman, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, General Cervenko, the other members from the clarification schedule, Norac, Ademi, Crnjac, Lausic, Jarnjak, Rebic, Radic, that they, one of them, had established a joint criminal enterprise, which included an accused. Well, how clear and definite is that evidence? We adopt the submissions of the legal team for General Gotovina which were heard yesterday. But we say with some force, looking back at this trial, what evidence has been produced that establishes so that you are satisfied, so that you are sure of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. Ambassador Galbraith was referred to. He was a man who had meetings. He was a man not from the Croatian government. He was a man who spoke to a large number of people and gave his impressions. Is that evidence that is capable of establishing beyond reasonable doubt of the existence of a JCE? We submit no. There is just as much in this case a reasonable inference that civilians, off-duty military personnel, combinations of civilians and military personnel. Perhaps military personnel ganged up together, going off to take revenge, loot, do what they do. But where, where is the evidence that establishes that this was a planned joint criminal enterprise beyond reasonable doubt? Our submission is this is yet another case theory that came about from internationals, had to be adopted by the Prosecution, and was adopted. And as part of those other points I have made today, these matters have been driven from the outside, not the inside on this case. And that is why, when you look back over the work of the last year and seek an answer as to where is the JCE? Where can we find it? It's not there. There are thousands of contradictory points to establish that there wasn't an JCE. I have pointed out to General Cermak reporting to Dzolic to go and see about fires that were happening outside Knin on the 9th of August, reporting him -- sending him to go and look because these matters had been reported to him by General Forand. Again, it doesn't add up, and if there is an reasonable inference the other way, this Court is not bound -- and this Court should not - because a reasonable doubt is there. Not a speculative doubt - this Court should not just plump for the Prosecution theory as against the other evidential foundation which indicates otherwise. Our submission to the background of this, it's not a speculative doubt that has been raised principally by the Gotovina legal team in challenging these issues; it's not a speculative doubt; it is a reasonable doubt. And, therefore, at this stage defeats the Prosecution allegation. Just as a point to add, I refer the Court to the Brdjanin appeal decision at paragraph 413, where it is stated: "In order to hold a member of a JCE responsible for crimes committed by non-members of the enterprise, it has to be shown that the crime can be imputed to one member of the JCE and that this member, when using a principal perpetrator, acted in accordance with the common plan. The existence of this link is a matter to be assessed on a case-by-case basis." And as was said yesterday, we start from the premise of the lawfulness of the operation. That was conceded by Ambassador Galbraith. And then we move from there to saying, Well, where did this joint criminal enterprise, then, come about? And was it ever there? Our submission is, evidence clearly indicates no. And referring the Court to the Haradinaj appeals decision, paragraph 137: "It must be proved that a common purpose, understanding, or agreement exists between the participants that they will commit a crime within the Statute." Now, I don't want to spend too much time here on the legal definitions; that is a matter for the Court. And I know they are experienced Judges fully resourced in relation to the law. And at this stage this is very much a evidential submission that the evidence is simply not there against General Cermak, and I will start with some overall matters, in relation to him. There's been positive evidence concerning General Cermak that he wasn't part of any joint criminal enterprise. That has been seen through the international witnesses, stating his door was always open. General Forand said that; transcript 4236. Always willing to cooperate; that was said by General Leslie. Many others. The Court will be aware of the assistance that he had given the UN, and the Court will remember that that was a specific part of his function as evidenced through the presidential transcript, when there is discussion about Knin, and it was said by the President, Well, General Cermak has gone down there to help the UN. And that was part of his role. And that's what he was carrying out. And one can see that he, at the start, goes to the camp where the displaced persons have grouped around the UN. There is an big problem for the international community, as well as the Croatian government as to what had happened with the collection of people at the UNCRO barracks. He meets the people. They seem, from the evidence, we haven't had a precise quota, I don't think, that they are mainly Serbs who is have gone there and Serbs who were living there under the previous regime. General Cermak asks - Exhibit P388 - "for a complete list of refugees, so I can see problems, see passes are issued to all who want to leave the camp and go on living in the area of Knin." Exhibit D311 General Cermak assists the UN in escorting 51 displaced persons from other UN camps in Sector South to the UNCRO barracks. Exhibit D38, General Cermak telling the Serbs in the UN camp to stay, not to leave Croatia. Exhibits P409, D146, D29, evidence of General Cermak telling members of the international community he wanted people to remain in their villages. There is the document that he gave to the Serbs in the camp giving them rights, emphasizing rights, saying what their citizens' rights under Croatia would be. This was not something that a person who wanted the forcible displacement of these people from the region would be doing, in our submission, if that was the purpose he attached himself to and was carrying out. I'm starting here because there's no evidence at all of General Cermak, when he was Mr. Cermak before the 5th of August, being involved in any shape or form in the acts, meetings, discussions, planning of events before Operation Storm. He comes into this case absolutely distinctly, from the 5th of August, and it is at that moment that he arrives as garrison commander into the picture. So absolutely no evidence of anything before. Very important, in our submission. This is a man put into the situation after the operation has taken place, and if one is to judge by his steps what he does, if he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise, would he be going so publicly and so bold into the UN camp, holding a press conference publicising the fact that these people should stay. If that's the plan, and he is doing this on national television, the Court has seen video evidence of him speaking in the camp, and at a press conference, telling people to stay, that they will be protected. Why would be doing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, Mr. Kay, something is moving and is producing some noise. I don't know what it is. It is perhaps close to your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll put the microphone that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then your voice still can be heard by the interpreters and the transcriber, then it's fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I won't ask if I need a microphone. Why would he be going on Croatian television and promoting these ideals if he was in a joint criminal enterprise? When you look at his function in the scale and scope of things if he was part of a plan to seek the removal of these people from the area. One could think of many other steps, if he was in a plan, that he would be taking, and it certainly wouldn't be issuing statements, encouraging them to stay. At the least, he would keep his mouth closed about it. But, no, the evidence indicates otherwise. This Court has to be sure that that was some kind of elaborate cover-up if it is to ignore and not accept his acts and conduct at the time that plainly contradict the joint criminal enterprise. And, look, this allegation was made in the case that he was denying crimes and effectively ignoring General Forand. Well, in fact, we have put into the Court, many statements from General Cermak where he acknowledged crimes were taking place. The fact that he doesn't agree it is an organised military plan but says it is civilians, or it is terrorists, or whatever other reason, is not a ground to condemn a man because he doesn't agree with the point of view of others from outside his country. This is not some kind of test as to whether you get it right or wrong. He admitted, throughout those human rights reports, to General Forand, to everyone, that there were crimes taking place, and he condemned them. But what seems to have happened here was that there was a belief that this man was able to do far more than he could actually achieve and deliver and was empowered to deliver. And that's what this case is about; that that impression was wrong. He was a man who had, no doubt, respect from the international community. But there became, as one can see, through the thread of evidence, a frustration that what he said would happen, that it would stop, didn't. That what he said would take place and certain people would be arrested may not have happened. But that doesn't mean to say that he is responsible for those crimes taking place, nor if the basis of his authority has been misunderstood, misjudged, maybe because of his own steps in actively dealing with the United Nations, helping them. It's not that that should condemn him. It's whether or not the acts and steps he was taking were part of a joint criminal enterprise. And we have this issue right at the start over whether he's military governor, or Zborno Mjesto, and the garrison commander. In a way, the titles don't matter. This Court is judging him by what he did. And when the Court is reminded of him being publicly stated in a newspaper interview on the 7th of September condemning the taking of apartment, houses, condemning crimes, how does that fit with him wanting those crimes to take place? He didn't have to do that. It was clear that the UN internationals were frustrated because General Cermak couldn't deliver his promises. And gradually they were able to form the point of view that he didn't have real power. They had doubts about him. And that's the point, Your Honour. He was down there helping them as the point of contact in front of them, and so he, naturally, as the point of contact, messenger or the receiver of messages, was the person who became condemned because results were not happening. In our submission, that is quite unfair to him and should not be how a case is judged. I'll remind the Court here of the terms of the paragraphs of the joint criminal enterprise alleged against him, starting at paragraph 19(a) just to see what we have had to face during this case, whether it makes sense, whether it adds up. Let's look at 19(a): "Issuing orders and directions concerning the administration and operation of the Knin garrison." How does that add up to being steps taken in furtherance of a joint criminal enterprise? How can issuing those orders that are all logistical, non-operational, even if you call telling Captain Dzolic to go and see why fires are taking place on the 9th of August, how on earth can any of that amount to being acts in furtherance of a joint criminal enterprise concerning the administration an operation of the Knin garrison? Well, we have combed and put forward virtually every scrap of paper, as the Court knows, from the 65 ter list and documents that we have found, and we asked this question: How any of that, anything that he did or said furthered the joint criminal enterprise as expressed in 19(a). Let's turn to paragraph 19(b): "Directing, facilitating, supporting and issuing orders to elements and/or members of the Croatian military, the police, or Croatian government Ministry of Interior, including the military police and civilian police." Well, we have covered large passages of this previously in my submission. The Court here has seen the orders produced during the evidence. They are all consistent with assisting the United Nations, assisting displaced persons, normalizing life in Knin, general garrison issues, how did any of his activities, if you collect them all together as exhibits, as we have, and look at them, and as we have put them into this Court during cross-examination as collections of documents, how do those steps taken by him rise to that level, whereby he has directed, facilitated, supported, issued orders, et cetera, in such a way that the object of the joint criminal enterprise being the permanent removal of the Serbian population has been realized? We submit it simply isn't there. Paragraph 19(c): "Permitting, denying, and/or minimizing the ongoing criminal activity, including participating in the reporting of false, incomplete, or misleading information regarding crimes committed while knowing that widespread destruction and plunder of property belonging to Serb civilians and the unlawful killing and inhumane treatment of Krajina Serbs were ongoing." This case concerning General Cermak is very different from the Brdjanin case, which was a case concerning inflammatory and extreme speeches by an accused and resulted in a conviction. The Prosecution have to prove that anything said by him furthered the alleged joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose of which was the forcible removal of the Serb population. How did anything said by him which could be even considered to be a minimizing statement be other than a point of view, an expression by him, just because he doesn't accept that this is an organised plan or that the military are responsible for committing crimes, just because he says, Well, this is revenge, there are civilians, and he says that to General Forand or Mr. Flynn or Mr. Al-Alfi, how does that further the joint criminal enterprise? This is a very judgemental indictment, in my submission. We get these complicated structures of allegations where we're having to deal with vast verbage, accusing someone of many activities, and the point of it becomes, often, lost. In our submission, none of what he said to the internationals, which were not denials of crimes. There may have been an occasion or two when he said, Well, I'm not sure that happened. That's not sufficient to form the basis to suggest because he doesn't agree with someone, that he suddenly entered a joint criminal enterprise. It's -- it's extreme to start judging people in that way. And in our submission, the construction of an indictment like this, making this wide variety of allegations without proving even that anything that came within 19(c) caused Serbs to, leave, prevented Serbs from saying -- from staying is fatally flawed. You have to tie this up. You can't just make these allegations and say, You did that; it fits with the pattern and picture of a criminal enterprise, and then not provide the basics and the reasoning, the connectivity to show that that had an effect and caused the common purpose to be achieved. In our submission, that simply does not happen in the way that has been expressed in this indictment. And why hasn't this case been structured in that way to establish it, that anything he said caused people to leave? Well, that's because the evidence simply is not there. It's not there. And it's taking a very extreme judgemental position on every single activity by an accused and then magnifying it into a form of criminal conduct that is not appropriate. You have to have a sense of proportionality, and that's the missing word for me in relation to an indictment such as this against Mr. Cermak. You may be able to criticise him for a decision he made or a statement that he made, but what has been proved concerning why he made it? Let's take the Grubori example. What has been proved concerning what he knew at the time. It is interesting that the first full report of the killings in Grubori came from the office, Captain Dondo, of the garrison. It completely contradicts the theory of General Cermak being involved in a JCE, if the people working with him report a full report of the matter to the police. Not only that, statements made by him on the Monday, on the TV in the video, what has been proved as to his state of mind, the information that he was in possession of? If you are going to start trying people about what they say, you have to go the full way and establish that what they said was a misleading account of the information in their possession. That has not been done in this case. General Cermak was entitled to take the position presented to him by the Ministry of Interior special police. That's how the country worked. This was not a military matter; this was a police matter. A report takes place. They give a report. It is not for him, in his function and role, to start questioning information that he has been given. Otherwise, every spokesperson for the troops in of Afghanistan, Iraq, the Falklands, wherever, would be responsible under this 19(c) for having committed an offence. You've got to prove that it was done misleading and it was with the intend of causing the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise to be perfected or to come about. And, in our submission, proportionality is what is needed in relation to these allegations to have any sense. In the last three minutes, I will now turn now, before the break, to paragraph 19(d): "Failing to establish and maintain law and order among and discipline of his subordinates and neither preventing nor punishing crimes committed against the Krajina Serbs." I covered this yesterday in my argument in relation to the Article 7(3) subordination issues. May I just point out that within the garrison regulations the word "law" is not present at all, and that has been an insertion in the indictment, if it is to refer to any obligations under the garrison regulations that is not to be found. The word "order" is different. His subordinates, as we know, nine, were the units of the Split Military District subordinated to him. Answer from yesterday, no. What were his duties to prevent, punish crimes committed against the Krajina Serbs? He had a duty to discipline his subordinates under Article 19, 27 of the Code of Military Discipline. Article 26 is as a superior officer, if an offender is brought before him, not of his organic unit, and it is necessary and -- I've forgotten the other words, necessary and reasonable or necessary and appropriate, word to that effect, for him to take minor disciplinary measures. For that, you look at Articles 5 of the Code of Military Discipline, et cetera. No evidence to support the foundation for this allegation as part of the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honour, that's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Just to inform you that you have approximately 45 minutes left after the break. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to briefly raise one matter. The Chamber was informed that there is an -- exists disagreement on the accuracy of P461, which is the transcript and translation of the Brioni meeting. We also have D1453 in evidence, but that is the cover page, and I do understand that there's no dispute about that. Now, instead of filing a -- another version of the transcript, the Chamber invites Defence or Defence teams who are not in agreement with the transcript and the translation, to just file a brief written submission in which it says, Having reviewed the -- P461, we put on the record that ... page this and this, line those and those, are not transcribed accurately. The Defence takes it that an accurate transcription would have been ... and then give your version of it. The same for translations. I don't know whether it covers half of the document or just a few lines, but then the Chamber is put on notice that there is dispute about the accuracy of the transcript and the translation, and if the Chamber wants to rely on the relevant portions or on the whole of the document in taking into account certain lines. So if they have real importance for the interpretation of this piece of evidence, then, of course, the Chamber will have to resolve it. I mean, we can't just say, Well, we take the one that is best for either Prosecution or Defence. Then either we have -- we need independent persons to listen to the text and to see to what extent the transcript reflects what is said. We can ask further opinion on translation. But to start with, the Chamber wants to know where's the problem and what is the problem. So the Defence, if they cannot reach agreement, and I do understand that no agreement could be reached with the Prosecution, is invited to put this on the record. And the Chamber will not just, because the status is not yet evidence, will not ignore what is said and say, Well, P461 is in evidence, so therefore that is the evidence and the other is not. That is not a formal approach the Chamber will choose. The Chamber would further like to be informed, both by Defence and by the Prosecution, and I think for the Prosecution we earlier, I think, we denied a request to have the -- to receive evidence on who transcribed it. Of course, the Chamber know what is was offered as evidence. At that time, we said we don't want, at this moment to be presented with this evidence. We gave the reasons for that. Now, unless we hear otherwise, the Chamber takes it that the view of the Prosecution is that the transcript provided at the time was produced by Croatian government officials, without further -- any further details. Now, if the Defence challenges it, of course, we'd like to know, on the basis of what; and who, if there`s a translation issue, on whose authority the translation is criticised. So we have transcript as one; translation is a second matter. Again, the Chamber will look at that time and see how important it is, not just focussing on the one or two lines -- two lines, but also what role these lines or these 10 or 20 or 50 lines plays in the interpretation of the document as a whole, and, of course, the parties can make submissions about the importance of those lines, but rather than to have now a new document in evidence, the Chamber will be confronted with exactly the same problem; that is, which is the correct one. And if there's any need to establish that, in relation to what is challenged, and the Chamber does not know yet what is challenged, of course, we'll try, in full transparency, try to resolve the matter. Any comments on this invitation? Parties consider it a suitable way of proceeding with this, and then we expect such a submission by -- I think it was the -- it was Gotovina Defence, but I'm not quite sure whether it is just the Gotovina Defence or other Defence teams as well, we'll hear whether the filing will be on behalf of Gotovina, or on behalf of Cermak and Markac as well. Then, Mr. Kay, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, turning now to paragraph 19(e): "Providing false assurances to the international community, that action to stop the crimes was being and/or would be taken." In our submission, there is no evidence Ivan Cermak provided false assurances, and we will be looking at the evidence in specific detail in a moment. No evidence has been provided to show that what he said he knew to be false. And let us look at the practical measures that were taken to stop crimes by the Ministry of Interior and the Croatian military, and look as well as what happened to crimes that were reported to him by the international community or whomsoever. Let's look first and consider the time-line of orders from the high-level Croatian authorities that were issued to stop crimes. And we say these orders by themselves contradict the JCE allegation. They are orders that plainly get more intense as troubles increase. And that of itself is interesting, as it indicates that what happened after the liberated territories were re-occupied by the sovereign authority, that this may not have been a matter that they had planned for or considered in advance as to what might happen, and that's probably the story of this case. From the 6th of August, Exhibit D323, General Cervenko issues the order for the purpose of preventing theft of property and undisciplined conduct. So when General Cermak says, Measures are being taken, we know that, on the 6th of August, the Chief of Staff issued this order which is a measure being taken. We know on the 6th of August, Exhibit D582, the police, the Ministry of Interior, dispatched forensic officers to police administrations for temporary assistance with forensic tasks at the Zadar-Knin police administration. So two arms of the Croatian system of government in operation on the 6th of August. Let us look at the 6th of August as well. General Gotovina himself issues an order, Exhibit D643, to control and process properly the spoils of war, and that indicates those three orders of how the system was thinking at the time. 7th of August, the Chief of Staff, General Cervenko, Exhibit D324, issues an order, prevent burning, looting, and all other illegal acts. 8th of August, Exhibit D583, Mr. Moric, follows up an order of the 4th of August, instructing heightened security measures for transport infrastructure and defence of the country. 10th of August, General Gotovina, Exhibit D204, issues an order on compliance with military disciplinary measures. And it says: "Take all necessary measures and fully engage in the implementation of the military disciplinary conduct and the maintenance of order in the area of responsibility and prevent arson and all other illegal acts. Take resolute measures against anybody who conducts himself in an undisciplined manner." Well, we know from evidence the background in this court as to what was happening in this area at the time. But were false assurances given by General Cermak in the background to these orders issued from the authorities precisely on the points of complaint by the international community? Why would these orders be issued if there was a plan that they should allow people to go and commit crimes with the object of expelling or removing the Serb population from the region? It doesn't add up. And can you see from what documents we have; we don't have every document in this case, but Exhibit D325, 10th of August, Commander Vukic, Operative Group Sibenik, issued an order, in order to prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and save human lives. Exhibit D644, an order from Captain Nakic, commander in Drnis replicates exactly the same wording from the previous order of Commander Vukic, compliance with measures of military discipline, in order prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and to protect human leaves. That's Exhibit D644. Well, that shows a system in operation, not a system failing. That shows assurances given by General Cermak that steps were being taken to control the behaviour of the people in the region were not false. Not false at all. This is the evidence. And the concern at the highest level of the Croatian authorities, on the 10th of August, Exhibit D46, Mr. Moric to General Lausic, so the Ministry of the Interior to the military police, asking him, Lausic, as chief of the military police administration, to take measures to eliminate burnings, lootings, killing cattle; also to increase cooperation between civilian and military police at check-points. So why, if the Ministry of Interior assistant minister with responsibility for the fundamental police is seeking cooperation and coordination with the military police and asking measures to be taken, and this proves the point of the separate hierarchical lines that Moric couldn't order Lausic, why would this be happening if there's some giant plan to enable people to commit crimes? 12th of August, Exhibit D205, Commander Kotlar, again using words taken from General Gotovina's order of the 10th of August. Exhibit 205 says: "Take all the necessary measures, preventing arson, looting, other illegal acts. Take stringent disciplinary measures against perpetrators of such acts." 12th of August, the Split Military District SIS, section for political activity, Exhibit D465, issues the warning to take measures to prevent burning, destruction of property, killing of livestock, theft, improper conduct, et cetera, and saying responsibility shall be with the commanders of units and political officials within units, and it's necessary to take punitive measures. 13th of August, Exhibit D646, order of the commander of the Gospic Military District: "Make maximal efforts to prevent looting, arson, et cetera." And they were concerned, because as in the previous exhibit this stated, "in order to prevent sanctions on Croatia that the international community threatens ..." Well, if the high-level Croatian authorities are supplying reasons to those beneath them, why crimes should be prevented and stopped because they are concerned about the international community, why on earth would they be supplying the reason if actually their plan was to affect these crimes through perpetrators under their order with the intent of causing the Serbian population to leave the area? It does not add up. It is not joined up. All these, I notice, are Defence exhibits that have gone into evidence as well. Let's go to another D number. 14th of August, Exhibit D647, Split Military District Command at Drnis. Implementation of the 12th of August warning to all assistant commanders for political activity of the 142nd Home Guard. Again, 14th of August, 112th Zadar Brigade. Implementing that 12th of August warning. Exhibit D648. 15th of August, Nakic at Drnis, Exhibit D649, forbidding burnings of residential and other structures, perpetrators will face disciplinary measures, and the commander of the unit will be relieved from duty. And then we get an intensification of effort from 17th of August as Mr. Moric, from the Ministry of Interior, issued what was Exhibit D48, produced by me to Mr. Flynn. And I produced this document about Moric writing to Lausic requesting a new plan of joint work to eliminate crimes because he described the perpetrators of these acts in most cases are persons "wearing Croatian army uniforms. There are also persons who are not members of the Croatian military but are only abusing the Croatian military uniform." Because this precisely underlines the point that this was not an organised activity but that this was activity arising from the release of pressure upon the liberation of the occupied territories by those who had been kept in circumstances where they were almost refugees in their own country who, for the first time, were allowed in their new state to go back to their areas and that this release of pressure was the reason why these people took revenge. But I introduce this following on from D46, showing Moric and Lausic at work, trying to deal with crimes. This is just a selection. There is more from the military police administration and elsewhere. But if we're facing the allegation that we were giving false assurances that action to stop the crimes was being and/or would be taken, it is important that these matters are brought to the Court's attention, because not only does it contradict the JCE, not only does it show that Mr. Cermak was telling the truth, but it shows that he was being misjudged in those international reports where officers of the international community, be they UNMOs, UNCROs, or whatever, were saying, He makes promises but nothing happens, that judgements have been made in ignorance as to the true state of affairs within Croatia at the time. And rushing to judgement which causes an indictment is a dangerous matter, and that's why, at this stage of the case, we say that there has been a rush to judgement on this, following the lead of the United Nations representatives out there. The Prosecutor rushed to judgement, took their opinion, did not investigate further and in detail and in depth, nor call the appropriate witnesses to determine this issue in a satisfactory way, nor produce the correct documents in trial that establish the truth, and a rush to judgement to say, Ah, this was not being dealt with by the Croatian authorities. In our submission, the background shows that the system was trying to work and issue orders, so far as it could, to the police and military, to stop what was happening. The problem is, however, that if components within the system don't listen, if components want to break the law themselves, what can you do? What can you do? There must be proportionality about this. The fact that crimes still happen doesn't mean that people have to be held into account. Here you're hearing about those steps that were taken to stop crimes. Going further, 20th of August, Cetina, in Exhibit D585, of the commander of the Zadar-Knin police administration asking the problem to be addressed of transporting goods and livestock through police check-points, taking care to prevent crime from being committed, taking livestock and protecting the property of citizens. We're not dealing, as the Court has heard, with a well-resourced NATO-style state borne out of the EU with all the regulations and controls that are in place. This was a new state, new ministries, new military, faced with a problem upon liberation that it was simply not fit for the purpose to deal with. That does not give criminal responsibility. Because the structures were not capable does not give criminal responsibility. It was able to liberate, but it was unable to regulate and enforce satisfactorily. It tried, and there are many examples of prosecutions and cases and reports of crimes in police log-books or military police log-books, and if there was a plan, none of that would be in existence, because that would not be the idea of putting the plan in operation. Well, these orders continue throughout August, and I will select one or two. The Court has had them all in evidence, 22nd of August, Exhibit D50, a document I put to Mr. Flynn. Mr. Moric, instruction to follow up on the 18th of August order concerning crimes being committed, including requests for specific information. All wanting to be handled at the highest level. Further, it goes through, all the days of August, 22nd, 24th. The administrations, the police administrations, the Ministry of Interior, all the way. Time doesn't permit me to go through these one by one till October. But it's there. The Court has had it, and we submit the Court should consider it, because it contradicts the evidence, and maybe it would be appropriate because this is analytical evidence if we made a filing on the matter before the Court in the same way that the Prosecution did just before the close of their case with the Kardum documents which Your Honours ruled upon as being admissible as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I perhaps, very practically, Mr. Tieger, would there be any objection against such a filing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me consult with -- first of all, I'd like to look at the Kardum to refresh my recollection on that. Secondly, just give us a brief opportunity to consider that, then can I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- perhaps later today would that be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if not, on Monday. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We offer it in the spirit of helping the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I should ask Defence counsel as well whether they would oppose the other Defence teams against such a filing. I hear of no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you to my learned colleagues. Let's look at specific reports of crimes and actions, then, that came to General Cermak. What is striking in this case is that there were many general reports as evidenced in the international's documents put to him, complaints about burning, arson, looting. As witnesses have said, well, it was obvious there were burning, arsons, and looting because you could see it happening. It was around. It was there. The Court knows that General Cermak, as part of his way of carrying out his normalization of life in Knin, had daily meetings to coordinate and seek cooperation. And these took people from all walks of life in Knin, as well as civil authorities, such as the police, as well as the military police, to enable people to be briefed. And in Mr. Gambiroza's diary or notebook, that's how it's described, as briefings as to what was happening. In our submission this seems a very responsible and correct way of performing if you are attempting to normalise life in this region. If you weren't bothered about crimes, why would you have the police there, or the military police? Let me remind you what -- what was said at the meetings concerning discussions of crimes. Witness 86, transcript page 5555. "There were discussions about crimes and matters within the jurisdiction of the police at the meetings. The problems discussed related Knin and the localities that gravitated towards the town of Knin." We know from the passage I pointed out from you from Captain Dzolic as to the fact that he had been referred to -- to investigate some burnings that were happening that could be seen from Knin on the 9th of August. All positive steps, all steps taken, so as to pass on information to enable people to act on that information, cooperation and coordination, not subordination, but information. And that information was to enable control of this area to be taken. When general crimes are just put before someone, what do you do? If General Forand says, Well, there's arsons and lootings happening around Drnis, how can you precisely deal with that, other than to report it and pass this information on at the daily meeting? So let's just have a look at positive steps taken. And you've had Exhibit P875, the statement of Captain Dzolic, about him going to see the commanders to tell them that burning houses was not to be tolerated and to take actions against the perpetrators. 9th of August, as we know, General Forand requests assistance from General Cermak to locate his three missing UN vehicles. Specific reference of a crime. You've seen the documents that resulted from that to assist the UN. Again, Exhibit D303, the particular vehicles are outlined. The history of that we have been through. Exhibit D505, 10th of August, 1995, the small shareholders company, notifying theft of assets. And General Cermak sends a report attaching the complaint by the small shareholders company to the Knin police administration, a referral of a specific matter. Exhibit P814 concerning the maltreatment by three Croatian army soldiers of an old Serb man called Drpa, Dusan; Dusan Drpa, who had come out of the UNCRO camp and had gone back to his home and received maltreatment and abuse. Referred to General Cermak by the international community, and he said that case was being worked on, and that would have been a matter raised in the daily meetings. We know of the Grubori matter where Captain Dondo, or Lieutenant Dondo, at Exhibit P1044, reports what he found at Grubori, as a result of this matter being raised with General Cermak and in fact being referred to the office of General Cermak on the 25th of August, and he reported that matter to the Knin police. Specifically, the 5th of September, Exhibit P383, and Exhibit 230. On the 5th of September, there was a protest concerning the murder of Sava Babic, delivered to the military governor of Knin as it was expressed in the report. In fact, at that time, as the notes of the meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi on the 7th of September show, General Cermak was not in Knin. However, Exhibit D230, on the 6th of September, 1995, Mr. Romanic, the chief of the Kotar-Knin police, refers the matter to the Zadar-Knin police to supply information. Again, on the 7th of September, 1995, when General Cermak, on that day, had returned to Knin, Exhibit P37, he is publicly stating in newspapers that crimes should not be committed. Described in Exhibit P829 of the 14th of September, 1995 as being a media campaign to stop illegal moving into empty flats, looting, and arson. Exhibit D487, dated the 27th of September, 1995, a report sent by Mr. Romanic, the chief of the Kotar-Knin police administration, at that time, to General Cermak, referring to a case of rape that had occurred on 8th of August in Knin discovered on 9th of August and informing him that it had been put before a judge in Zadar and for other incidents in Gosic on 27th of August, Brgud on 10th to 11th September, et cetera. 3rd of October, 1995, Exhibit P1169, the issue of the killings in Varivode, where nine people were killed on the 28th of September. This wasn't dealt with by General Cermak, as he was out of town but by the deputy, Gojevic. Let's see if Gojevic, the Deputy Commander of the Knin garrison acts appropriately. He advises that this was found out by him on the 29th of September and that all information should be obtained from Zadar police, who were investigating as of the 28th of September of 1995, and this matter was being dealt with on a daily basis. And the Varivode investigation can be seen at Exhibits P268, P278 as being matters that were being dealt with and investigated. And on the 11th October 1995, Exhibit P1223, a letter from General Cermak to Carmen Burger of the International Red Cross referring to a specific case that had been referred to him and what was happening. Well, we know he is not in charge of the civil police. We know he is not in Knin and has no authority and responsibility to go around investigating crimes. But matters that are reported to him as specific matters are all dealt with, and the evidence shows it. Perhaps there are one or two that weren't; but, again, this is a sense of proportionality that we have to have in this case. We know that there were the daily meetings where crimes were discussed as a point on the agenda. Again, in our submission, this shows that these matters were being dealt with and are -- an entire contradiction of the case that has been brought against this accused. Why would these steps taken if he was part of a joint criminal enterprise? It simply doesn't add up, and the Court, at this stage, is entitled to rule that and stop these proceedings. There's no point in just keeping everybody happy by allowing it to continue when the evidence does not fit that which has been alleged. This is an entirely different set of circumstances, revealed in the evidence during this trial in this case, to what has been opened by the Prosecution and presented as their case in their indictment and the pre-trial brief. Just general matters about the joint criminal enterprise, Article 7(1), in our submission, no evidence of planning, instigating, ordering, et cetera, as described in these very wide and general terms within the indictment. Your Honour, my time now has come to an end. But we submit that through the course of the evidence in this case, we have shown that this is an entirely different situation to that which has been expressed by the Prosecution as being criminal conduct by this accused. And, in fact, the acts taken by him, positive steps taken by him, show that he was doing just that which he was described as doing by countless witnesses, and that was the normalisation of life, helping the civil authorities. It was not doubt thought that putting a civilian in uniform and sending him down to this non-operational role would have been of assistance to achieve those ends for all concerned at that time. If he was being given any greater status or responsibility, aside from being a civilian in uniform in a non-operational post, he would have been given some grand title and command post. He has been given a grand title, and that was by the internationals, and that was because of a misunderstanding as to the nature of his actual title and role. He was given the title of military governor and all that implies to those western internationals as to what a military governor can do in a region. But that wasn't the case here. That was not part of the establishment of the Croatian government, such a position and post, and I'm not being critical of people at the time, but I do say that a little bit of research, thought, and consideration of matters in a more detailed manner at the time may have led to a far different outcome and understanding of the nature and role of this man who was a civilian in uniform. Your Honours, those are my submissions on behalf of Ivan Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. For the Markac Defence, I see, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you're on your feet. May I take that you'll be the one or the first one to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be the one to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have an opportunity to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, this is the Markac Defence 98 bis submission. I will not -- I will endeavour not to repeat much of what my colleagues have said with respect to the standard of review. My colleague, Mr. Akhavan adequately covered the standard review, and it is well known to the Court. What I will like to highlight for the Court in our 98 bis submission deals with joint criminal enterprise issues, the 7(1) allegations, and the issues of command responsibility of General Markac under 7(3). There will also be some additional issues that I will discuss after that command responsibility issue, but in general, the bulk of my submissions today will deal with JCE and command responsibility. Paragraph 12 of the amended indictment allegations that General Markac, among others, participated in a joint criminal enterprise 1, category 1, "the common purpose of which was to remove permanently the Serbian population from Krajina." This conception allegedly occurred on Brioni on the 31st of July, 1995, and it was implemented through Operation Storm. The implement ation of this joint criminal enterprise, as alleged to have occurred on the basis of large-scale indiscriminate artillery attacks. Indiscriminate shelling is the pillar of the Prosecution's joint criminal enterprise theory. The shelling, it is alleged, was followed by large-scale destruction, appropriation, and discriminatory measures which were aimed at allegedly preventing displaced persons from returning. In addition to these crimes which constitute the category 1 JCE, the indictment alleges by way of JCE category 3 that it was foreseeable that the crimes of murder, inhumane acts and cruel treatment were a possible consequence in the execution of the enterprise. Your Honours, the Prosecution in our humble submissions has tried in vain to make the case for indiscriminate shelling. The area of Knin obviously has been covered at great length by my colleagues from the Gotovina Defence, and I will not cover that. What I will, however, cover is the shelling claim made with respect to the special police in its axis of attack. There is absolutely no evidence, none, to support the claim that the special police's use of artillery was indiscriminate in its axis of attack. Specifically, let's focus on the village of Gracac. We have no evidence; there is no witness who has testified that there were any civilian casualties in Gracac, as a result of shelling. There is it no evidence and no witness to quantify any civilian collateral damage as a result of the shelling of Gracac, or that civilian buildings or civilians themselves were targets in Gracac. There is no witness who has testified that General Markac had anything to do with planning and preparing the artillery operations in this axis of attack. There is no doubt that the special police did not have territorial responsibility, unlike the Military Districts of Split and Gospic. There was no territorial responsibility. There was no zone of responsibility. The special police had specific tasks enumerated for them which were ordered by the Main Staff of the Croatian military. They were front line troops. They did not occupy territory. As soon as Operation Storm was over, they were recalled for other duties. As a matter of fact, on the issue of artillery, the only testimony concerning artillery for Gracac specifically comes Mr. Turkalj, Prosecution witness, who testified, among other things, that he had instructions to ensure that civilians would not be in harm's way as far as artillery was concerned. He identified military targets within Gracac as was confirmed by Witness Rajcic. Mr. Turkalj testified that only 130-millimetre cannons were used, that multiple rocket launchers were not used, even though they were at his disposal, and that roughly for the town of Gracac itself, 15 rounds of artillery were used. These transcript references are at 13697, 13703 to 707. Moving further on into the axis of attack of the special police in Operation Storm is the village of Donji Lapac. Now, the only testimony about shelling with respect to Donji Lapac is that the special police, according to Mr. Turkalj, the only person who has testified about artillery with respect to the special police, did not use artillery in the fighting to liberate Donji Lapac. And that transcript reference, Your Honours, is 13713 to 16. As a matter of fact, the only shelling that occurred in Donji Lapac was the result of Serb shelling from Bosnia and from friendly fire, both of which occurred on August 7th. P614, which is the special police war diary, discusses both of those events. The war diary shows that Donji Lapac, on the 7th of August, was liberated at 1300 hours. At 1410 hours, the special police suffered a heavy artillery attack from its HV artillery firing from positions in the Udbina area which stopped at 1440. P614 continues that the special police were already gone from Donji Lapac by 1630 of that day and towards Kulen Vakuf in Bosnia, and that the Serb artillery opened fire on Donji Lapac from Bosnia at 1945. As far as Gracac and Donji Lapac are concerned, the claim that Gracac was 85 per cent destroyed and Donji Lapac was completely destroyed by members of the special police forces, as claimed in the Prosecution's opening statement, has no evidence to support it, with respect to the special police. But let's not rely on the Prosecution's opening. Let's hear from the Prosecution's artillery expert, Mr. Konings. What was his testimony on the issue of shelling and the special police axis of attack, specifically Gracac? He had no opinions at all, critical. Or even a discussion of the special police and its use of artillery in Operation Storm. The indictment alleges that as part of the joint criminal enterprise, General Markac used artillery at his disposal. How that artillery became part of a joint criminal enterprise has gone undiscussed in the evidence from the Prosecution. The Prosecution, according to Mr. Konings himself, did not even ask him about specific issues relating to the use of artillery in Operation Storm by the special police, including targeting issues. That's zero evidence on a pillar of the Prosecution's JCE claim on shelling, with respect to an entire axis of attack in Operation Storm. With respect to the Brioni meeting, other than being present at the meeting and having no substantive issues discussed by him, although there was some discussion of General Markac, how does the presence of General Markac at that meeting constitute membership in a joint criminal enterprise? Where is the evidence of General Cermak's mens rea? What is the crime? The Prosecution, in its opening statement conceded, as it has throughout this case, that Croatia's right to reintegrate occupied territory into its internationally recognised borders was not in dispute. Yet the Prosecution has utterly failed to present one shred of evidence of how the special police artillery attack in its area of operation, in its axis of attack, constituted intent to commit a crime, and through that crime made a significant contribution to the commission of a joint criminal enterprise. Let's look at the specific documents relating to the special police vis-a-vis Brioni. Exhibits 535, 53 -- D535, D536, and D543 are documents which discuss the special police, orders from the Main Staff of the Croatian military to the special police regarding operations that they will conduct in the axis of operation which occurred during Operation Storm. D535 is dated June 26th of 1995, more than a month before the Brioni meeting. This document of the Main Staff ordered the Ministry of Interior special police to launch attacks from the operations base in the area of the Velebit mountains, with the aim of taking control over the area of Mali Golic, Sveti Rok, Gracac, it was to cut off the Gospic-Gracac road, take control of the Celavac radio relay facility, place the pass and tunnel in Prezid under surveillance, and link up with the Split Military District forces. The operation as stated in June of 1995 was to be carried out in two stages over the period of three days. Almost immediately after this specific order, the Main Staff issued another order, D536, essentially negating the previous order of June 26th. What happens on July 29th? D543, another order from the Main Staff to General Markac, stating exactly the same -- almost exactly the same as the order of June 26th of 1995. The MUP special forces shall carry out an offensive from the operations base in the area of Mount Velebit, in order to take control of the area of Mali Golic, Sveti Rok, Gracac, Prezid. What were the objectives of that order, which allegedly was the result of a joint criminal enterprise? Cut the Gospic-Gracac road between Sveti Rok and Stikade, seize the Celavac radio facility, put the pass and tunnel at Prezid under observation, link with the forces of the Split Military District. The operation shall be carried out in two phases and shall last three days in all. Before the Brioni meeting, after the Brioni meeting, the order is exactly the same. This, Your Honours, with respect to General Markac, Shows that, A, he was not involved in any planning; B, he was not involved in any joint criminal enterprise. Let's look at what the real significant contribution of the special police was, as described by General Forand in P401. General Forand discussed the success of the special police and said as follows: "We have to recognise that the Croatians had tremendous strategic success and that their small special force units did successfully accomplish special missions." Forand goes on to state that: "The key action in the HV campaign in Sector South was in the Velebit mountains at Mali Alan." And as am aside, Your Honours, the civilian population in this mountain area of Mali Alan was zero. Forand continues: "We know from JORBAT and UNMO reports that HV special police battalions had been training and operating in the Velebits for some months. On 4 August, three of these battalions about 1.000 men, supported by heavy artillery fire, took the crossing through the Velebits along the Mali Alan road that lead toward Lovinac." Forand continued: "The HV exploited this success and advanced almost unopposed to Gracac and then further east, thereby cutting off Knin and the south of the Krajina. This hub of road junctions effectively controlled all north/south communications in the Krajina and could be qualified as a strategic success." That's the real contribution of the special police in Operation Storm, as described by General Forand. General Forand interestingly in the same document, P104, with respect to the civilian population, does not mention anything about shelling causing them to leave. What he does say in this report is: "One must ask himself why the RSK decided to order the civilian population to flee, unless it was already a foregone conclusion."
