Even more interesting when not manipulated through the prism of the Prosecution's indiscriminate shelling accusation is that Forand states, and I quote: "Their use of artillery was excellent, but the coordination between artillery, tanks, and infantry was not evident." For Operation Storm General Markac was operating in a narrow axis of attack. He was responsible to the Main Staff of the Croatian military in Zagreb, with respect military tasks and objectives. When Operation Storm ended, his tasks changed at the orders of the Main Staff. These orders specifically are contained in D550, and D551, because initially his objective was only as far as Gracac. But when the speed of the advance became such that stopping might allow the retreating RSK to set up a second line of defence, he was ordered by the Main Staff to continue his pursuit, eventually to the state border of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a task that the special police completed successfully, with minimal casualties, with minimum civilian collateral damage, all with the goal in mind to liberate Croatian territory and to restore Croatian sovereignty. Now, on this particular territory of Sector South, between August 10th and August 21st, the special police was not present. Under order of the Main Staff, D557, they were withdrawn to Petrova Gora, in Sector North. They were not present for 11 days. D559 is an order from the Main Staff to the Croatian military to conduct certain mop-up operations due to armed resistance that was going on, not specifically to the special police, but to the military. D561 is an order asking the -- ordering the special police to return to Sector South to conduct certain mop-up operations. With respect to the civilian -- to the special police, we have had no evidence that the displacement of civilians and the special police axis of attack or anywhere else that the special police was located resulted from grounds not permitted in international law as required by Articles 5(d) and (i). There is no evidence to sustain either the Prosecution's joint criminal enterprise theory of liability at Brioni with the intention of terrorising and expelling civilians on discriminatory grounds or to sustain the Prosecution case that the crimes of persecutory unlawful attacks and deportation were in fact committed irrespective of the existence of a JCE. We've heard no evidence, none, that proves discriminatory intent on the part of General Markac. There is no document; there is no statement; there is no conduct on his part. There is no witness testimony that provides any evidence of discriminatory intent for General Markac towards Serbian civilians on the ground of their ethnicity. As discussed by my colleague Mr. Akhavan, with respect to the murder and inhumane and cruel treatment allegations under Counts 6 through 9, there can be no JCE 3 attributable to General Markac without evidence of JCE 1. If we look at the JCE 3 claim, the key issue here is foreseeability on the part of General Markac that crimes of murder, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment were a possible consequence of the execution of an alleged joint criminal enterprise. There is no evidence provided by the Prosecution of a common state of mind for the alleged co-perpetrator as is set forth in Krstic. Krstic at paragraph 613 states: "If the crime charged fell within the object of the JCE, the Prosecution must establish that the accused shared with the person who personally perpetrated the crime the state of mind required for that crime. With no evidence of foreseeability or common state of mind beyond mere pleadings and arguments, this mode of liability must fail." Now, the Prosecution in its opening statement claimed: "From that the virtual outset of entering towns and villages, the special police began committing crimes." We have no specific evidence from any source that identifies the special police as committing crimes while entering towns and villages, engaging in any wide-scale burning or looting at all. None. This leads me into this next section of my 98 bis presentation, which I call guilt by proximity. In this section we have a variety of witnesses who testified that they thought they saw the special police and identified them by uniform only to be wrong time and time again. In addition, the Prosecution puts the special police via these witnesses in cities and villages in which they never set foot, according to the war diary, P614.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I was discussing before the break, I was about to get into a section that I call guilt by proximity with regard to the special police, and this dovetails somewhat into what Mr. Kay discussed regarding the construction of the indictment and the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. In many instances there is discussion of special police being close or at or near instances of where crimes were occurring. What is very telling about those accusations, however, is we have heard no evidence that anyone reported the special police to any competent authorities for participating in, allowing, or acquiescing in burning and looting. There is not one single shred of evidence that anyone reported the special police to any competent civil authorities for acts such as those. Moreover, along the lines of guilt by proximity issue, there is not one single meeting that has been -- was requested of General Markac. The internationals that we have heard parade through the courtroom over the course of the trial, there is not one single person who even knew who General Markac was much less requested a meeting with him. So with respect to issues relating to guilt by proximity, it is our submission that the special police were not involved in any kind of guarding or looting or burning. As a matter of fact, the testimony itself by many witnesses, and I will cite some examples here, as I said earlier, were asked to identify their version of what they call to be the special police by uniform, only to be wrong time and time again and to put them in places in which P614, the special police war diary, does in the even have them present. For example, witness Hill was asked at transcript 3773, 3773, lines 18 through 21: "Q. And the individuals you saw in the town of Pecane, were they both individuals wearing these uniforms as well as others? "A. These uniforms, and I believe, the dark blue of the special police around those vehicles." So we have Mr. Hill identifying the special police in dark blue uniforms. And then we have Mr. Williams who testified. In his statement, if you recall, he discussed seeing the special police in Knin on 5th and 6th of August. He was asked. "Q. Sir it's a fact," at 9642, line 13, "that you have no idea whether or not the Croatian special police were in Knin on the 5th and 6th of August; correct? "A. I cannot confirm that special police were there or not; that's correct, sir." Later on he was at 9645, line 20. "Q. With regard to the special police, they had single coloured uniforms. What was the colour of their uniforms? "A. To the best of my recollection, it was sort of an off greyish steel colour. "Q. What kind of head gear did they wear? "A. Berets. "Q. What colour? "A. Black, to my knowledge." So we off grey steel with black berets. Witness Mauro in a report P27 relating to Grubori, which I find highly instructive, at page 12064, referring to the report: "A HRAT which travelled to Grubori on the afternoon of 27 August has received reliable reports of a group of 10 camouflage-clad Croatian special police moving up the road to Grubori mid-morning on 25 August." So we have now camouflage coloured special police. Witness Al-Alfi at 13940: "Q. Have you ever seen, yourself, the special police forces? "A. Oh, yes, while they are -- but I did to the talk to them. They have a special dress. It's a special uniform. "Q. What colour? "A. I'm not sure. It can be blue; it can be dark grey, something like that. But I knew that. So we have Al-Alfi describing the special police in blue or in dark grey. Witness Bellerose at transcript 5875: "Q. You described these soldiers as Croatian special police. Can you describe for the Court what they were wearing. "A. They were wearing one or two-piece uniform that was either going from memory dark grey or black. They were also wearing black load-bearing vest." Later on in his transcript at 5951: "The soldiers were usually wearing fatigue uniform with camouflage pattern, and those persons stopping us, I call them the special police, were wearing a one-colour uniform either very dark grey or black." So we have yet another colour describing the special police by Witness Bellerose. At 5955, Witness Bellerose states at -- was asked. "Q. You cannot tell me what factual basis you came to conclude that these people who stopped you were actually Croatian special police; correct? "A. I was assuming by their uniform." Now, the only witness who correctly identified the uniform of the special police was Witness Steenbergen. Witness Steenbergen was in Gracac on the 5th of August 1995. That's when the special police were on their way there during Operation Storm. He was asked at 5425: "Q. Did you observe the clothing that these persons wore that was part of this group when you spoke to the commander? "A. Yeah. They were wearing olive-green military suits. The commander was wearing a Kevlar helmet, and they were wearing OPS vests." Now despite the pictures that we have seen of the special police in Gracac, and we have seen photographs of them, we have continued to have evidence led by the Prosecution either through the pre-trial brief or through witnesses, that people identified as special police were not special police. To fit their theory that special police were present in areas in which burning and looting were occurring. There is no referral of the special police by any of those internationals that we have discussed with respect to burning and looting in any town or village. With respect to issues -- oh, one other thing I need to add regarding uniforms. And I think it is the probably the coup de grace on the issue of uniforms, was the Leslie radio interview. The Leslie radio interview in which the question was put to General Forand about the interview, and in the interview Leslie said: "There were a variety of organisations," at 4433 in the transcript, "that then swept into this former Serbian Krajina. There were special police teams wearing their very distinctive blue uniforms who were engaged in hunting and killing in the mountains of Serbian civilians. We have another witness uninformed witness on the issue of the special police and what their uniforms look like. With regard to specific issues related to planning, there is no evidence that General Markac either planned Operation Storm, artillery attacks on any front, much less Knin, no evidence that he was involved in post-Storm planning or operations, other than specifically ordered mop-up operations directed by the General Staff of the Croatian army after August 21st. Not to speak of no evidence of his planning, initiating, ordering or committing crimes. All of his activities were reported to the General Staff. And it's my submission, Your Honours, with respect to the joint criminal enterprise claim against General Markac that the 98 bis submission should be granted. I will now turn to the issue of command responsibility under Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As I stated, I will turn to the 7(3) command responsibility issue. The key issue with regard to General Markac and command responsibility is this: There is no evidence that General Markac had knowledge of crimes that were not known to civilian authorities who were responsible to undertake measures. First, in relation to liability for Counts 6 to 9, based on command responsibility under 7(3), there is no evidence to support the Prosecution theory that General Markac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish crimes which were alleged to have been committed by his subordinates. There is no evidence to show that General Markac had any ability to conduct crime prevention, crime investigation, or crime prosecution. It is a distinction with a difference. Because, unlike the military, which had its military police and its military courts, General Markac had no such apparatus at his disposal. Quite the contrary, with respect to General Markac. When such crime investigation was brought to his attention by the competent civilian criminal authorities, he acted. And I refer you specifically to Exhibit D530, D531 and D1078. D1078 describes specifically what happens in a situation where General Markac is informed by the competent civilian authorities that a special police member is under a reasonable suspicion to have committed a criminal act. D1078 specifically describes: "Since there is an reasonable suspicion that the above-named had committed a criminal act; since criminal proceedings are being conducted against him at the investigative centre of the Zagreb county court, the special police member was suspended." Looking at D530 and D531, General Markac requests that the Knin-Zadar police administration handle an issue initially referred to him. It was referred to him via an Official Note, and we have a heard a lot of discussion about Official Notes, from the Gracac police station, that there was an allegation of a burning incident involving members of the Zadar special police. Once this was referred to the Zadar special police, the local commander there determined that the facts established that one of the members of the unit had committed the act, and the local commander was the one to impose the discipline. Now, with respect to Grubori, the end is justifying the means. And what I mean by that is we began with the Prosecution proposition in the opening statement of the Prosecution regarding Grubori, and this is the conclusion that's reached. The true story -- and I'm quoting from the opening statement: "The true story is that the special police murdered the victims and destroyed the village. And that, together, Generals Markac and Cermak worked to ensure that this would never be known." "Never be known." The internationals were there at the moment it occurred. Literally, half of Sector South, and that might be a exaggeration but ... "They were there after the event, and it was broadcast to the media the next day. A video camera is in the village on the day of the event showing some of the homes that were on fire. With respect to Grubori, General Markac sent his Chief of Staff, Mr. Sacic, there after the event to see what happened. You've heard that this was a mop-up operation in the area, in which this village was located; this mop-up operation being under the command of the staff in Gracac. To this day, no one has determined precisely what has happened in Grubori. No one. Not the special police, not the criminal police, not the Croatian government, not the internationals. No one. There is only a conclusion. A conclusion that has not been backed up by specific facts. You've heard that the mop-up operation was one of many occurring, that the special police conducted. We've heard multiple versions of this event presented here in court by multiple witnesses. The interesting thing about witnesses the Prosecution has chosen with respect to the special police to testify here are that not one of them was in the village during the course of the action. Not one. Mr. Janic testified he was in the vicinity; he did in the go through the hamlet of Grubori. Mr. Celic testified he was in the vicinity. He did not debate through the village of Grubori. Mr. Turkalj who was the commander of the Lucko Unit, which was allegedly involved in this operation, testified. He didn't come there until the day or two after. Mr. Turkalj was present there, HRAT, UNCIVPOL, Croatian civil police, all of these people were present there after the event. The Prosecutor talks about an alleged cover-up. When looking at the situation as whole, it begs the question: What was being covered up? Grubori was out in the public eye. There is a picture of an infirm man lying in a pool of blood. There is an claim now known not to be true through the testimony of Dr. Clark that another man in Grubori had his throat slit. That story was promoted everywhere and ended up not being true. The UN was there, as I said, UNCIVPOL, the Croatian civilian police, the press, television, the incident was recorded in the log-book of the Knin police. It was passed to the Zadar-Knin police administration in Zadar. Yet the civilian police under whose authority an investigation was to be conducted did not undertake a crime-scene investigation, if it in fact believed a crime had occurred there, as it was obligated to do. To this day, the testimony as that there are more questions than answers about what happened in Grubori, yet the competent responsible authority for determining what to do there, the civilian police didn't do its job. There is no evidence, none, that demonstrates it was General Markac's responsibility to conduct a crime investigation or crime prosecution with respect to Grubori. In fact, the only evidence given by the Prosecution on Grubori is that it was the responsibility of the crime police to conduct the investigation. We heard that from Witness Zganjer. We heard from that Witness 84, and we heard that from Witness 86. They were to conduct an investigation, bring a investigative judge and competent prosecuting attorney. Nevertheless, when informed that something had occurred in Grubori, General Markac did not bury his head in the sand. He asked his Chief of Staff to look into the event. Let's look at the testimony of witness Zganjer for a moment. Mr. Zganjer was asked on page 11609: "Q. Do you know that special police members are not the element of the police force that carries out crime investigations? "A. Yes. Special police has clearly defined tasks interviewing citizens or suspects conducting crime-scene investigations, taking other operational crime-investigation measures. These are not the tasks of the special police, that's for sure." With respect to an issue of a cover-up, the only testimony here with respect to a cover-up is that there was not one. And that is from Mr. Zganjer. The question was asked of him on page 11610: "Q. As you conducted actions on the Grubori case, did you come across any facts that indicated that there was an attempt to cover up or to in any other way tamper with the investigation from any side. In that case you would have had to institute criminal proceedings against such a party? "A. Yes, quite naturally. In such a situation, I would have tried to clarify all the circumstances in which this attempt to tamper or cover up of this whole incident by those persons was carried out." And the follow-up question to that: "Q. As you dealt with the Grubori case while you were the state attorney in Sibenik, did you ever obtain any evidence or learn anything to the effect that General Markac did anything to, in effect, prevent any investigation into the Grubori incident and clarification of the circumstances of the incident? Did you come across any traces of this activity on the part of General Markac? "A. From the materials that I had at my disposal, I was unable to establish any facts that would indicate that I should reach such a conclusion, the conclusion that Mr. Markac had in any way prevented or obstructed the actions of the police regarding the Grubori incident." Now, there was some discussion with Mr. Zganjer about the fact that his investigation in 2002 was a long time after Grubori had occurred. His position was that the police could have done something before 2001, and that after his investigation he learned that not only a criminal report hadn't been filed but not even a regular report with regard to Grubori. He found obviously that the report had been entered the in Knin log-book but that no one had done anything with it. That goes in the testimony of Witness 84. Witness 84 was the person who entered this incident first into the log-book. And Judge Kinis asked him a question, several, on 11427 of the transcript: "Mr. Romassev came to your office and provided you information regarding the incident of Grubori. Did you ask him to show where this area is located in the map? Answer: "I did not. There is something you need to keep in mind. Once I received the information, I immediately went to inform the coordinators and my head." Then there was a break. "As I confirmed, it seems we did not act appropriate as the police force. We were supposed to react and do our job. Whether we did or not, that needs to be assessed. As of the moment I received the information from Mr. Romasev we should have acted. We did not, at least not mold, and I don't know why, though."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS FURTHER ASKED
utterances.text: "Did you have specific instructions provided to you how to handle with information with dead bodies which are found in the area, or should you follow the rules of criminal procedure law in that respect?" Answer: "In my view, what we -- what needed to be done is to investigate each and every incident, in particular, when bodies were concerned and where one can conclude with a degree of certainty that the military was involved. Then a team was supposed to go out immediately, investigating and submitting a report to the administration." Judge Orie with this witness at 11113: "Witness 84, at that time, having received that information, what went through your mind about what to do or what not to do? Could you tell us. Answer: "Well, if I had had the ability to take charge, my first step would have been to inform the duty operations officer which had been done in fact, later. Then I would have requested that the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb and their duty operations service be informed immediately, as well as the police administration in Zadar, and their duty operations service. And then Zadar, as being in charge of criminal investigations should have been asked to set up a team, including an inspector, a homicide inspector, a scene of crime officer, and another person to go and perform an on-site investigation. If that had been done, I believe it would have been possible to identify the perpetrator, and all this discussion today would not have been necessary. Those are the basic police actions that should have been taken then. Why this has -- this hasn't been done, I really don't know, nor can I give you any precise information. There was a problem with this case, but what kind of problem, I don't know. Why it all turned out this way, whatever I said would be a guess and could be a wrong guess." So the police, in this particular instance, did not do its job. Mr. Markac has nothing to do with the civilian police. What was the reasonable and necessary measure that General Markac failed to take with respect to Grubori? He had his Chief of Staff, Mr. Sacic, look into what happened. You asked -- ask yourself what about Celic? He said that nothing happened. Well, it is clearly obvious that in Grubori something happened, and it was obvious when General Markac had Celic come in to see him that all General Markac wanted was to find out what happened. Sacic concluded, based on his review that there was an armed conflict in which there were civilian deaths. What evidence is there that Markac could not rely on information gathered by Mr. Sacic as being accurate? It is reasonable for a commander to rely, and they're entitled to rely on the information provided to them by their subordinates. You heard Mr. Turkalj testify that to him, it appeared there was an armed conflict in Grubori after having been at the scene. That is what it looked like to him based on his combat experience. The operation itself was conducted under the authority of the staff in Gracac. There is no evidence that General Markac had command of the mop-up operation being conducted in the area in which Grubori was located. The members of this unit which allegedly went through this area in which Grubori was located were responsible to Celic. Celic's immediate commander was Janic. Josip Turkalj was in command of the Lucko unit. Sacic was the Chief of Staff in charge of the mop-up operation in question. Those are commanders four times removed on levels below Markac on the command scale. General Markac is not a clairvoyant like the Prosecutor would like to make him out to be. If in fact there was a wall of silence among those who were in Grubori, what could he do about it? He could not suspend anything without any criminal charge, without any specific evidence that they were involved in a crime, upon the information received from his Chief of Staff that there was an armed conflict that occurred in and around Grubori. He could act on two occasions: Upon an Official Note or criminal charge by the competent civilian authorities which had the authority to conduct investigations provided to him, or report from the commander of an operation that a crime had occurred. Of those two alternatives, none happened. The only person who did anything with respect to this was General Markac. He asked for his Chief of Staff to look into the situation. The fact is that to this day, we have no answer for what happened in Grubori. The investigation is still open. And what the Prosecution has done with respect to Grubori is to cover up its inability to provide the Chamber with evidence beyond reasonable doubt that General Markac, the man furthest removed from the event, was somehow responsible for Grubori with the allegation that he covered it up. There is no evidence that what happened in Grubori was ordered by General Markac. There is no evidence that what happened in Grubori was covered up by General Markac. And there is no evidence that he had the authority to punish anyone under him with what he knew at the relevant time. You're only as good as the information you receive. He is -- was entitled to rely upon the information that he received from his subordinates. Now, there is some discussion about the internal control mechanism, and that is a mechanism that allows General Markac supposedly to be able to discipline people. Let's look at what the evidence on internal control is with respect to the Prosecution witness Janic who testified extensively on this issue at P6234. He was asked: "Q. Mr. Janic, do you know that the sector for internal control conducted any disciplinary procedures? Or did it instigate or process disciplinary measures against members of the special police? "A. No, that was not within their jurisdiction concerning the internal order within the Ministry of Interior. And I may say that the same situation prevails today. Disciplinary proceedings were instigated by unit commanders or superiors. If have you a police station and a policeman from that station commits a misdemeanor, then the head or chief of the police station will launch disciplinary proceedings." Similarly, according to the same principle, the person authorised to instigate disciplinary proceedings within the special police was the commander of a specific unit. So one of his responsibilities was to institute disciplinary proceedings for disciplinary breaches within his units. If I were to commit one, then the disciplinary proceedings against me would have to be instigated by the head of the sector. However, the internal control sector did not have within its pursue any competence or authority to institute disciplinary proceedings. In addition, Mr. Janic confirmed that the special police did not have its own disciplinary court at 6247, lines 14 and 15. With respect to issue of 7(3) command responsibility, it is our submission, Your Honours, that the Prosecution has presented no evidence that General Markac had any knowledge of crimes that were not known to the civilian authorities upon whose responsibility it was to undertake measures. That's the key issue here. As a result, this mode of liability must fail and a judgement of acquittal must be rendered. There are two small areas, Your Honours, which I'm going to cover very briefly. The first can be handled in a sentence or two, and that's the issue of armed conflict, which no one has really discussed yet. At paragraph 55 of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges that at all relevant times, a state of armed conflict existed in the Krajina region of the Republic of Croatia. We have not seen one document, one witness, or any other evidence that there existed an actual state of armed conflict after the close of combat operations in Croatia in Operation Storm. For intents and purposes, Operation Storm ended on August 10th, 1995. Combat operations essentially were over. We have no witness, no evidence to testify that a state of armed conflict existed after that date. We discuss that issue extensively in our pre-trial brief, Your Honours, but I won't discuss it any further at this point. As to the scheduled killing incidents, there is no evidence that General Markac had any involvement in scheduled killing incidents 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9. I have discussed scheduled killing incident 4. We will reserve our discussion on the 189 additional alleged victims, but I can state with respect to General Markac that at this point there is no superior/subordinate relationship that he has with respect to any of the alleged killing incidents that I have discussed. In conclusion, Your Honours, Count 1 persecution requires the highest amount of mens rea. A conscious attempt to discriminate against Serbian civilian merely due to their ethnicity. As Kupreskic case tell us, this is it one step removed from genocide because there is no evidence and there no evidence that has been put forth on the issue of discriminatory intent, Count 1 persecution must fail. On Counts 2 and 3 regarding deportation and forcible transfer, the shelling is what is the bottom line issue on Counts 2 and 3. There is no evidence that anyone in the axis of operations or attack of the special police fled due to any unlawful shelling. Counts 4 to 9 of wanton destruction, pillage and plunder, cruel treatment, and murder under Article 3, General Markac did not have the intent to commit these crime against humanity or war crimes through destruction and pillage of property, nor did he make a significant contribution to the commission of such crimes. We have not heard any evidence of what the significant contribution General Markac made under Counts 4 and 9 -- through 9. As is evident through the area of attack that General Markac was commanding, there was no widespread attack against civilians. As a matter of fact, the speed with which they advanced prevented them from sitting and occupying towns and villages. They kept moving forward. They took Gracac; they kept moving forward. They went on to Otric, and they went on to Bruvno, and Mazin, and Donji Lapac. All these areas on foot, 60 kilometres from Mali Alan in the Velebits to the Donji Lapac, mostly on foot. There was no time for them to sit and burn places down, and no time for them to sit and loot places because they were on the move. They were always on the front. They did not maintain law and order. They did not maintain anything by the front line. They kept moving. Because there was no widespread attack against civilians, Your Honours, and certainly not in the special police axis of attack, the Article 5 claims against General Markac must fail. Now, 98 bis provides that at the close of the Prosecution case, the Trial Chamber shall, not must or can, but shall, by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions, I'd enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. Your Honours, we believe our submissions show there is no evidence with respect to General Markac. For these reasons we respectfully ask the Trial Chamber for a judgement of acquittal of all counts in the indictment, because the Prosecution has failed to present evidence beyond a reasonable doubt in its case in-chief of General Markac's criminal liability under the amended indictment. Thank you, Your Honours.
